case.case_title: Saranapala v. Solanga Arachchi, Senior Superintendent of Police and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 470/96 (FR), decided on 18 June 1997

clause.text: No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the selective prohibition of the NSSP procession constituted discrimination against the petitioner on the ground of political opinion in violation of Article 12(2).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that the police discriminated against him and his party on the basis of political opinion by prohibiting their procession while allowing others.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the prohibition was based on security concerns and lawful police powers, not on political opinion.
key_facts: The NSSP procession was prohibited citing security reasons.
Other political parties were allowed to hold processions and meetings on May Day.
The petitioner and his party were treated differently from others without a valid security justification.
The petitioner adduced evidence including affidavits and photographs showing differential treatment.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court interpreted Article 12(2) as prohibiting discrimination on grounds including political opinion. The selective prohibition of the NSSP procession, without credible security justification and while allowing others, amounted to discrimination based on political opinion.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found the respondents failed to prove a genuine security threat justifying the prohibition. The evidence showed differential treatment of the NSSP compared to other parties, indicating discrimination on political grounds.
principles_established: Discrimination on political opinion violates Article 12(2).
Police powers must not be used to suppress political expression.
Burden of proof lies on the State to justify restrictions on fundamental rights.
precedents_cited: Joseph Perera v. The Attorney-General (1992) 1 Sri LR 199, 214, 218

outcome.holding: The Court held that the respondents discriminated against the petitioner on the ground of political opinion, violating Article 12(2) of the Constitution.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The State was ordered to pay the petitioner Rs. 15,000 as costs.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(2) was crucial in establishing that the police's selective prohibition of the NSSP procession was discriminatory on the basis of political opinion, which was central to the Court's decision to grant relief.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: By permitting members of other political parties to march while denying or seriously abridging the petitioner’s right to march, the respondents failed to act even handedly ... and thereby violated ... Article 12 (2) not to be discriminated against on the ground of political opinion.
